domains.title: Agent context
domains.statement: MCP surface serving parsed-codebase context to AI agents: tool registry, gating, response bounds.

domains.title: Cloud workspace
domains.statement: Team cloud: workspaces, members, auth, push/sync, CI auto-updates, distribution.

domains.title: Delivery analytics
domains.statement: Delivery-intelligence surfaces: canonical spine, dashboards, classifiers, and their trust rules.

domains.title: Extraction
domains.statement: Profile-driven code extraction: engine, substrates, profiles, and graph output contracts.

domains.title: Code graph
domains.statement: Rebuildable code-graph storage and query: backends, snapshots, IDs, freshness.

domains.title: Intent overlay
domains.statement: Repo-local product-intent overlay: capture, review, authority, and bounded agent context.

features.title: Create a cloud based workspace
features.statement: Owner can create cloud workspace on the platform

items.title: Accepted items survive capture byte-for-byte
items.statement: A capture that encounters an existing accepted item preserves its payload and authority exactly and records the proposal as a separate candidate.

payload.observer: Maintainer comparing the overlay before and after capture
payload.condition: Capture runs against an overlay containing accepted items
payload.requiredOutcome: Accepted payload and authority are unchanged; the proposal becomes or updates a candidate

items.title: Capture writes candidates only
items.statement: Anything an agent extracts or updates enters the overlay as a candidate; only an explicit maintainer decision can set accepted, rejected, or superseded.

payload.condition: An agent extracts or updates intent
payload.requiredOutcome: New or changed assertions carry candidate authority; authority changes are maintainer edits

items.title: Default context returns accepted current intent only
items.statement: Context requests without explicit authority filters return accepted current items; candidates require an explicit opt-in and rejected or superseded items are reachable only by exact id.

payload.observer: Agent consuming get_intent_context or the intent CLI
payload.condition: An agent requests intent context without authority filters
exceptions: Exact-id fetch may return rejected or superseded items
payload.requiredOutcome: Only accepted current items are returned by default

items.title: Late automatic releases are refused per repository
items.statement: An automatic release whose deployment time is older than the repository's latest unrolled release is refused with release_out_of_order and writes nothing; the deployment time is a property of the deployment itself, never of the record attempt.

payload.observer: The release ledger and its Postgres integration tests; a maintainer reading history sees no out-of-order delivery.
payload.condition: An automatic record arrives with an ordering token older than the latest unrolled release of the same repository.
exceptions: Human records keep the expected-head check instead
Releases of different repositories never order each other
payload.requiredOutcome: The record is refused by name with both tokens, nothing is written, and the refusal is logged with the deploy and PR identity.

items.title: Merged PRs keep only the plans they wrote
items.statement: An intent item is planned by the connector exactly while an open, non-draft PR names it in its Delivers trailer, or while the merged PR that wrote its active plan still awaits delivery or was restored by a rollback; any other merge never keeps a plan alive.

payload.observer: The delivery Postgres integration suite (plan lifecycle cases).
payload.condition: The connector re-evaluates plans after a PR opens, changes, closes, reopens or merges.
exceptions: Maintainer roadmap plans are never withdrawn by the connector
payload.requiredOutcome: Plan and withdraw events converge on the set of open non-draft PRs plus the PR recorded as the plan's provenance; drafts neither plan nor hold plans; a malformed trailer edit keeps the last good sets.

items.title: The overlay carries product statements only
items.statement: Stored and returned intent contains product statements, source references, semantic relations, and code ids only; source bodies, prompts, transcripts, credentials, and arbitrary files never enter it.

payload.observer: Workspace owner auditing the git-tracked overlay
payload.condition: Intent is stored or returned on any surface
payload.requiredOutcome: No source bodies, prompts, tool transcripts, credentials, or arbitrary file payloads are present

items.title: CI refuses to upload a degraded snapshot rather than overwrite a good graph
items.statement: When a CI parse produced no resolved call or external-call edges because the type-resolution tier could not run, the CI runner refuses to upload the snapshot before any push happens, so the workspace keeps its previously published graph.

payload.observer: The CI run itself — the pre-upload assertion in the CLI CI runner, with the refusal visible in the job logs
payload.condition: A CI parse completes without a working type-resolution tier, so the resulting snapshot has no resolved call or external-call edges
exceptions: A dry run parses without pushing and is unaffected
payload.requiredOutcome: The CI runner detects the blocking extraction degradation after parse and aborts before uploading; nothing reaches the push surface, the workspace keeps the previously published graph, and the run fails with the refusal so the missing prerequisite is fixed

items.title: Raw graph queries pass an allowlist, never a deny-list
items.statement: A raw graph query is admitted only if every clause it contains appears on an allowlist of read-only constructs and it is a single statement; anything else is refused before execution.

payload.observer: The query guard shared by every raw-query surface, which returns an explicit refusal to the caller
payload.condition: An agent submits a raw graph query through the query tool or the equivalent REST surface
exceptions: None — a construct that is not recognized as read-only is refused rather than allowed
payload.requiredOutcome: The query is admitted only when it matches an allowlist of read-only clauses and is a single statement; mutation, cross-database, filesystem, extension, and administrative constructs are refused before execution, and a second engine-level check stands behind the allowlist rather than replacing it

items.title: Raw graph querying is available by default only where tenant isolation is structural
items.statement: The raw graph query tool is offered without an operator opt-in only where isolation is structural, and every backend or hosted surface whose isolation depends on query-level narrowing stays behind an explicit operator opt-in.

payload.observer: Tool registration on the local server and the per-call capability check on the hosted server, which returns a visible capability error rather than a server failure
payload.condition: A surface decides whether to expose the raw graph query tool
exceptions: An operator may opt in on a shared-graph backend, accepting that the query sees the whole graph
payload.requiredOutcome: The tool is listed automatically only when the selected graph is structurally isolated to the caller's scope; on a shared graph or any hosted surface it is listed only when an operator has explicitly opted in, and on a backend with no query surface it is absent entirely

items.title: Scope decides what is visible; current repo only decides where the agent stands
items.statement: The configured scope is the only thing that bounds what an agent can see, while the current-repo setting is a vantage hint that ranks and defaults results without ever narrowing that boundary.

payload.observer: The agent issuing the query — a tool call carrying an explicit scope argument always overrides the vantage, so the agent can widen to the project or pivot to a sibling repo.
payload.condition: An agent queries the graph with a configured scope and, optionally, a declared current repo.
exceptions: In a multi-tenant cloud deployment the vantage travels per request as a header rather than as process configuration, with identical semantics.
payload.requiredOutcome: Visibility is decided by the scope alone; the current repo only makes single-origin answers report that repo's own dependencies and rank it first among same-named symbols, and it is ignored when the named repo is outside the boundary.

items.title: Service tokens record only automatic releases
items.statement: A service token holding intent:release may record a release only with the trailer body and only on a workspace in deploy mode; baseline, rollback, plan, withdraw and reinstate stay human actions, and changing the trigger mode requires workspace:manage.

payload.observer: Guard-level tests over the real HTTP guards.
payload.condition: A request to POST an intent release or to change the trigger mode arrives with a service token.
payload.requiredOutcome: The human body shape, any other kind, and any mode other than deploy are refused with release_mode_forbids; a mode change without workspace:manage is refused.

items.title: Source code never reaches remote storage
items.statement: Any path that sends graph data to Coredoc-operated remote storage must strip source code before the write, and a rejection by the remote guard is fixed at the producer rather than by relaxing the guard; on-prem clients may permit source storage inside their own infrastructure.

payload.observer: The server-side no-source-code pipe rejecting a push, or an audit finding source fields in remote tables.
payload.condition: Graph data is pushed from a local machine to any remote backend or shared cloud storage.
exceptions: An on-prem deployment runs entirely inside the client’s own infrastructure; the client may permit source storage there. The rule binds Coredoc-operated cloud storage.
payload.requiredOutcome: Source text is removed before the remote write; if the server-side guard rejects the payload, the producing code path is fixed and the guard is left intact.

items.title: Stable ids survive content edits; only versioned ids move
items.statement: A node's stable id must stay identical across re-parses of unchanged structure so graph relationships and cross-repo links hold, while the versioned id carries the content checksum and is the only part allowed to change when code content changes.

payload.observer: Cross-repo and impact tooling — a re-parse at the same parser version producing different ids, or previously linked graphs losing their links, is the failure signal.
payload.condition: Code content changes, or the identifier formula, its inputs, or path normalization is edited.
exceptions: A deliberate format change accompanied by a documented migration and version bump recorded with the change.
payload.requiredOutcome: Content changes move only the versioned id; a change to the stable-id formula or its inputs ships with a documented migration in the same change, otherwise it is reverted.

items.title: Summarization is optional and its failure never blocks the graph push
items.statement: AI summarization is an optional step of an automated run, and when no key is configured or the model is unreachable the run continues and still publishes the parsed graph.

payload.observer: The automated run command, whose reported result carries summarization statistics only when summarization ran
payload.condition: An automated run reaches the summarization step with no model key configured, or the model call fails
exceptions: A failure of the parse or the push itself does fail the run
payload.requiredOutcome: The step is skipped or abandoned and the run continues to push the parsed graph; only the summaries are missing, and previously computed summaries stay reusable for unchanged code

items.title: Sync result names unlinked repositories
items.statement: A connector sync result names every repository whose pull requests it ingested without a link to a workspace repo that carries an intent repo key, with the count of pull requests ingested from it; an empty list means every ingested repository was linked.

payload.observer: The connector_sync job result and the importer unit suite.
payload.condition: A sync ingests at least one pull request from a repository the workspace does not hold, or holds without an intent repo key.
payload.requiredOutcome: The result carries an unlinkedRepos list with one entry per such repository (owner/repo and the count of ingested pull requests); the list is present and empty when every ingested repository is linked.

items.rationale: Since the connector refuses intent events for unlinked pull requests, the refusal must be visible where the sync is observed (the job result), not only in the server log — absence is a first-class state, never a silent zero.

items.title: Telemetry is opt-in, off by default, and never carries a path, repository name, or source
items.statement: No surface emits telemetry unless the user has opted in, the opt-in is re-checked at every emit, an environment kill switch overrides it, and no emitted event carries a filesystem path, repository name, or source code.

payload.observer: The shared telemetry client that every surface routes through, which is the single place the gate and the scrubbing are applied
payload.condition: Any product surface reaches a point where it would emit a telemetry or usage event
exceptions: Full-detail attribution to a cloud workspace is a separate consent from anonymous product telemetry, and neither implies the other
payload.requiredOutcome: The event is emitted only when opt-in is currently on and the kill switch is unset; otherwise it is silently dropped. Emitted payloads carry no filesystem path, repository name, or source content, and flushing is bounded so telemetry can never hang a command

items.title: Workflow capture never sends raw prompts, tool payloads, source, paths, or spec bodies off the machine
items.statement: Agent-workflow capture may report sanitized usage and workflow events only; raw prompts, tool arguments and results, source, filesystem paths, and specification bodies never cross the machine boundary, and an export that cannot be sanitized fails closed.

payload.observer: The capture runtime on the machine and the workspace read surfaces that scope results by role
payload.condition: An agent session on a supported host reports workflow or usage events to the workspace
exceptions: None — an unsafe export fails closed instead of degrading to raw transmission
payload.requiredOutcome: Only sanitized events leave the machine — raw prompts, tool arguments and results, source, paths, and spec bodies are excluded — and any export path that cannot guarantee sanitization is disabled rather than sent; workspace-wide statistics are visible to administrators while a member sees only their own

items.title: Automatic intent release recording
items.statement: Coredoc records plan, withdraw and delivery events for reviewed intent from Coredoc-Intent-Delivers and Coredoc-Intent-Retires trailers in a pull-request body, according to the workspace trigger mode, so a maintainer no longer enters releases by hand.

payload.outcome: A change that carries the two trailer lines becomes planned when its PR opens, withdrawn when it closes unmerged, and effective when it reaches production, with the actor, PR and ordering token recorded on every event.
payload.boundary: A PR without trailers produces no events; rollback, baseline and roadmap plans stay human actions; validity of the trailers is decided only by the server parser.
payload.beneficiary: Maintainers who ship intent through pull requests, and agents that read effectivity before implementing.

items.title: Analyze a codebase entirely on the developer's machine
items.statement: A developer can parse, store, and query their code graph entirely on their own machine, with no cloud account and no code leaving the laptop.

payload.outcome: A queryable code graph — structure, entrypoints, data layer, call and import edges — produced and served locally by the CLI, a local database file, and a local MCP server.
payload.boundary: Local mode covers a single machine only: sharing with teammates, member management, and hosted MCP are cloud features, and moving to cloud is an explicit user step, never an automatic upgrade.
payload.beneficiary: An individual developer, and the AI agent working in their editor, who needs codebase understanding before trusting the product with anything shared.

items.title: Product-intent overlay beside the code graph
items.statement: A maintainer keeps a small reviewed product-intent model in the repository, linked to the current code graph, so agents receive bounded, applicable product context for a task.

payload.outcome: Accepted applicable items are returned together with whatever anchor and freshness evidence exists, including unmapped items
payload.boundary: Local opt-in pilot for one single-repo project; no cloud sync or collaboration
payload.beneficiary: Maintainers and AI agents working in the repository

items.title: One generic engine plus a per-repo declarative profile, not a bespoke parser
items.statement: A repository is extracted by a small declarative extraction profile that an AI authors and a human reviews, applied by one generic engine over a shared tree-sitter and SCIP substrate.

payload.outcome: A reviewable per-repo profile describing that repo's conventions — decorators, ORM operations, dependency-injection style, entrypoint conventions, external-client matchers — which the shared engine applies to produce the parsed graph.
payload.boundary: Language- and framework-specific logic lives in the profile, never in the engine or the substrate; there is no parser-generation command, and profiles are authored through the author-profile skill.
payload.beneficiary: The maintainer onboarding a new repository, who reviews and iterates a short declarative file instead of reading or debugging generated parser code.

items.title: Read-only code-graph tools for AI agents
items.statement: An AI assistant reaches the parsed code graph through a Model Context Protocol server offering read-only discovery, understanding, impact, and cross-repo tools.

payload.outcome: An agent can describe a repository and its database schema, search symbols, explain a symbol, list entrypoints, find callers and dependents, analyze change impact, and trace a call across services — without reading the whole codebase.
payload.boundary: Access is read-only over already-parsed data: the tools never mutate the graph or the repository, and answers are only as fresh as the last parse and push.
payload.beneficiary: An AI coding assistant, and the developer relying on it to scope a change before editing.

items.title: Zig repositories are extracted by a language target
items.statement: A repository's Zig sources are claimed by a zig language target and extracted into file, package, container-type and function nodes with stable ids, so the local graph and the read-only agent tools can answer what types and functions a Zig codebase contains.

payload.outcome: A ZigProfile, or a zig target inside a MultiTargetProfile, claims the repo's .zig files and the parse emits files, one root package, classes for struct/union/opaque containers, enum nodes for enums, and functions and methods, every id minted by the shared id generator.
payload.boundary: Uses the bundled tree-sitter Zig grammar; no semantic index exists for Zig, so no call, import, entrypoint, data-model or cross-language edges are produced in this slice.
payload.beneficiary: A maintainer onboarding a Zig repository and the AI agent querying it through search_symbols, list_file_symbols and explain.

items.title: A Zig file with top-level fields is a struct whose top-level functions are its methods
items.statement: A Zig file that declares at least one top-level container field is emitted as a class named from the file basename, with its top-level fields as properties and its top-level functions as methods of that class; a file without top-level fields is a namespace whose functions stay plain functions.

payload.choice: Emit the file-struct as a class when the file has at least one top-level container field; its top-level functions become methods with classId pointing at it. The @This() alias alone does not trigger the rule.
payload.question: Every Zig file is implicitly a struct. Should a file that declares fields be a graph class with its top-level functions as methods, or should top-level functions always be plain functions?
payload.rationale: Matches how Zig code names these functions and keeps nested-struct and file-struct treatment consistent.
alternatives: No synthetic file-struct node: top-level functions are plain functions everywhere and top-level fields are ignored
consequences: Method ids take the form method:<path>:<File>.<fn> for file-structs, so the rule cannot change later without an id migration
A namespace helper and a type method are distinguishable in the graph
The rule keys on observed data shape (fields present), not on file-name casing conventions

items.rationale: Zig code refers to such functions as Config.init, and the rule mirrors how functions nested in a named struct are treated. The choice fixes stable ids, so reversing it later requires an id migration.

items.title: Keep every delivery-analytics surface blameless — no per-person aggregates
items.statement: No delivery-analytics surface aggregates by person; attribution is by subsystem, work item, or process stage, and labels render as confidence-scored leading indicators rather than verdicts.

payload.choice: No delivery surface aggregates by person. Attribution is by subsystem, work item, or process stage; a work item's title or key is identity enough, and actor identity exists in the canonical model for linking only, never for ranking. Labels render as confidence-scored leading indicators, not verdicts.
payload.question: Delivery intelligence joins planning, code, review, and agent-session data — enough to rank individuals; should any delivery surface aggregate by person?
payload.rationale: Ranked-people dashboards corrupt the data they read — people optimize the metric and stop linking work honestly — and turn a diagnostic tool into a surveillance tool. Keeping the grain at subsystem, item, or stage preserves honest linking and keeps classifier data trustworthy, even though managers will keep asking for per-person views.
alternatives: Per-person aggregates and ranked-people dashboards, as managers request
Per-person views gated behind a permission or opt-in rather than excluded outright
consequences: Easier: honest linking because nothing is scored per person, classifier data stays trustworthy, and adoption inside teams improves
Harder: "who is slow?" is answered as "which stage or subsystem is slow" instead — by design
Commits every future dashboard, export, and API read to subsystem or item grain

items.title: The cloud graph is an immutable published file selected by an atomic pointer, not a mutable remote database
items.statement: On the Ladybug file-snapshot data plane, a cloud workspace graph is built as one immutable versioned file, published with create-only semantics after source stripping and verification, and made live by an atomic active-version pointer swap that readers open read-only.

payload.choice: Dump-and-swap: verified inputs build one immutable graph file, cross-repo edges are resolved inside that private file, the file is published to object storage with create-only semantics and never overwritten for the same identity, and an atomic compare-and-swap of the active-version pointer makes it live. Readers download, verify, cache, and open the selected version read-only. Source and embedding input text are stripped before publication.
payload.question: Interactive writes into a mutable per-workspace remote database degraded badly under realistic push sizes; how should a cloud workspace graph be produced and served?
payload.rationale: Incremental interactive writes against a remote mutable database made push latency unbounded and left graphs in degraded states, whereas a whole-graph rebuild published as an immutable artifact makes every read a known-good version and makes rollback a pointer change.
alternatives: Keep incrementally mutating a per-workspace remote database, with chunked commits to survive large pushes
Publish mutable snapshots that are overwritten in place under a stable key
consequences: Easier: readers always see a complete verified version, and rollback or promotion is an atomic pointer change
Harder: any change means rebuilding and republishing the whole graph rather than patching rows, and old versions accumulate until they are collected
A published version is content-identified and never rewritten, so a bad build is superseded rather than fixed in place
The decision governs the Ladybug file-snapshot data plane only; a Neo4j backend remains a mutable database outside these semantics

items.title: The desktop app is the primary distribution and entry point
items.statement: The product's primary distribution and user entry point is the desktop app, while the web app remains a frozen proof of concept with no active development, superseding the earlier web-first strategy decision.

payload.choice: The desktop app (apps/desktop) is the primary distribution and entry point; apps/web stays a frozen POC with no active development.
payload.question: Which surface is the product's primary distribution and entry point, given the 2026-07 strategy declared the desktop archived and the SaaS web-first?
payload.rationale: The desktop app was restored and is actively developed as the real product surface, while the web POC never left its proof-of-concept state; the strategy document's web-first direction no longer matches how the product is built and delivered.
alternatives: Web-first SaaS with the desktop app archived, as locked by the 2026-07 strategy document
Developing both surfaces in parallel as equal entry points
consequences: The 2026-07 strategy's desktop-archived decision is superseded and the strategy document is a historical record
Design, QA, and onboarding effort anchor on the desktop surface; DESIGN.md stays anchored on apps/desktop
The web POC receives no feature work and is not a supported entry point
The trunk-promotion runbook and export-verification tooling tied to the old strategy were removed

items.title: Every aggregate degrades explicitly — a missing source is never a silent zero
items.statement: Absence, truncation, and gating are first-class rendered states on every analytics aggregate, never rendered as zero.

payload.choice: Absence, truncation, and gating are first-class rendered states, never zeros: availability flags on graph-fused reads, a distinct disabled sentinel for feature-off, "based on N of M" captions on any limit-bounded roll-up, null metrics rendered as explicit empty states, and small samples flagged as directional.
payload.question: Analytics surfaces read sources that can be absent, stale, truncated, or gated — how should an aggregate render when its source is unavailable?
payload.rationale: A dashboard that renders 0 for "unavailable" teaches users that its numbers lie, and one such cell poisons trust in every other cell. Rendering the degraded state explicitly keeps a displayed number a measured number and makes "why is this empty?" self-serve.
alternatives: Render a silent zero when a source is absent, stale, truncated, or gated
Hide unavailable cells entirely, without telling the reader they were dropped
consequences: Easier: users can trust a rendered number is a measured number, and debugging an empty cell is self-serve
Harder: every new read must design its degrade states up front — an unavailable-source path is part of the feature, not an edge case
Commits new endpoints to carrying provenance such as availability and sample size alongside values

items.title: Machine-derived rows are re-derivable and prunable; human labels are ground truth and never auto-deleted
items.statement: Delivery rows split into two lifecycles: machine-derived rows are deterministic functions of canonical data and may be pruned and re-derived, while human-entered corrections are ground truth that is never auto-deleted and wins over machine output.

payload.choice: Two classes with opposite lifecycles. Machine-derived rows are deterministic functions of canonical data: safe to prune when their producer no longer emits them and safe to re-derive at any time. Human-entered corrections and labels are ground truth: never auto-deleted, never reselected for reclassification, and they win over machine output wherever both exist.
payload.question: The delivery pipeline derives rows from canonical data and also lets humans correct machine labels — what deletion and re-derivation rule applies to each?
payload.rationale: Derived rows go stale when detectors and resolvers improve, and without a deletion rule they become permanent ghosts; deleting human input would destroy the only data that cannot be recomputed. Splitting the lifecycles lets detector improvements converge the data automatically while protecting the irreplaceable half.
alternatives: One lifecycle for all rows — either never prune anything, or prune derived and human rows alike
Let re-derivation overwrite human corrections when the classifier improves
consequences: Easier: detector and classifier improvements converge the data automatically by re-derive plus prune, and reverts are safe by construction
Harder: any new derived table must declare its natural key and its producer so pruning is possible
Human-labeled rows can outlive the conditions that created them and need occasional human curation

items.title: Never inline a specific client's patterns into shared infrastructure
items.statement: Shared infrastructure carries no client-identifying material and no behavior gated on a detected client or framework identity; anything client-specific is config-driven or lives in the client's own artifacts.

payload.choice: Shared infrastructure — engine, plugins, templates, docs, test fixtures — carries no client-identifying material: no client org or repo names, product domains, or domain vocabulary, and no behavior gated on a detected client or framework identity. Examples use neutral placeholders; anything client-specific is config-driven or lives in the client's own gitignored artifacts.
payload.question: Features are built and validated against specific pilot repos while the engine, plugins, and docs ship to arbitrary customers — may a client's names, vocabulary, or patterns live in shared infrastructure?
payload.rationale: Client names, orgs, domains, and vocabulary leak naturally into examples, fixtures, CI templates, and heuristics, which is a confidentiality violation and a portability bug at once. Neutral, config-driven shared infrastructure can be shipped to any customer without a scrub pass.
alternatives: Inline client-specific patterns, names, and vocabulary directly in shared code, fixtures, and examples
Allow client material in shared artifacts and rely on a scrub pass before shipping
consequences: Easier: shipping any artifact to any customer without a scrub pass, and examples stay meaningful to every reader
Harder: writing examples takes deliberate neutralization, and real-client validation results must be recorded with placeholders
Commits reviews to treating a client identifier in shared code as a defect, not a style issue

items.title: One auth architecture — self-hosted OAuth issues every token, the upstream identity provider is pluggable
items.statement: A single self-hosted OAuth 2.1 authorization server issues tokens for every deployment mode, with the upstream identity provider selected per deployment and workspace membership managed natively rather than synced from an external directory.

payload.choice: One auth architecture: the self-hosted OAuth 2.1 authorization server issues tokens everywhere, and the upstream identity provider is a pluggable provider object chosen per deployment. Membership is managed natively through members and invites, including a pending state, instead of being synchronized from an external directory.
payload.question: The cloud product and the on-prem package each grew their own authentication path; should they keep separate auth stacks or converge on one?
payload.rationale: Two auth stacks means every MCP, CLI, and web surface is written twice and diverges; a single issuer with a pluggable upstream lets cloud and on-prem share one token model, one guard layer, and one verification seam while still meeting different identity requirements.
alternatives: Keep the directory-sync auth stack for cloud and the self-hosted authorization server for on-prem
Standardize on a single hosted identity vendor for all deployments
consequences: Easier: MCP, CLI, and web surfaces authenticate identically in every deployment mode
Harder: a new deployment's identity requirements are met by writing an upstream provider, and the authorization server becomes a load-bearing component the product must operate
Directory-driven membership management is not available; membership state lives in the product

items.title: On-prem ships as a generic sellable package, never as a per-customer deployment
items.statement: The on-prem offering is a generic, source-protected, self-installable package — first-party chart, published images, and documented install and upgrade paths — and no customer receives a bespoke deployment.

payload.choice: On-prem is productized: a first-party deployment chart with a documented values schema, product images in a private registry with per-customer pull credentials, an air-gap installation path, and source protection that relies on the private registry and the licence rather than obfuscation. Licence enforcement never bricks a running installation and nothing phones home.
payload.question: The first on-prem installation was built around one customer's infrastructure; should on-prem stay a bespoke engagement or become a product?
payload.rationale: A per-customer deployment cannot be sold twice and makes every upgrade a bespoke engagement, while a generic package with its own chart, release pipeline, and install docs is repeatable; refusing to phone home or disable a running cluster is what makes the package acceptable in regulated and air-gapped environments.
alternatives: Keep on-prem as a bespoke per-customer deployment built on the customer's own infrastructure conventions
Enforce licensing by remote check-in or by disabling a running deployment on expiry
consequences: Easier: a new on-prem customer installs from published artifacts without bespoke work, including with no registry egress
Harder: the product owns a deployment chart, a release pipeline, and install/upgrade/sizing documentation as first-class surfaces
Licence expiry can only restrain new issuance, so revocation of access is a business process rather than a technical kill switch

items.title: PR body is the only source of delivered intent
items.statement: The fact that a change delivers or retires specific intent items lives in the pull-request body as trailers and nowhere else; the ledger records what it reads there and no server table duplicates it.

payload.choice: Git-style trailers in the PR body, id@version per item, read by the connector and by the CI step.
payload.question: Where does the mapping from a change to the intent items it delivers live?
payload.rationale: A second authoritative store drifts from the PR for many reasons; the body is reviewed, versioned and already ingested.
alternatives: A server-side table of planned deliveries written by the review stage
Deriving deliveries from commit messages
consequences: The review handoff must render the trailer block
A malformed trailer refuses the release rather than being reinterpreted

items.title: A precision-first extractor is verified by anti-scenarios + graph-wide invariants, never coverage bars
items.statement: Verification of a precision-first extractor must carry anti-scenarios, graph-wide property assertions over the whole output, and a blind adversarial review as a gating phase; coverage counts, recall rates, and random samples may inform a retro but never stand as the precision bar.

payload.choice: For any extractor whose contract is precision-first, verification carries three things beyond coverage: anti-scenarios pairing every emitting scenario with a "must NOT emit wrong-X for adversarial input Z" twin under a named failure hypothesis; graph-wide property assertions over the whole output rather than a sample; and a blind adversarial review as a gating phase whose confirmed correctness findings block done. Coverage counts, recall rates, and random samples may inform the retro but never stand as the precision bar.
payload.question: An extractor whose contract is "false output is worse than missing output" cannot be validated by instruments that measure coverage — what must its verification carry instead?
payload.rationale: A plausible-but-wrong edge increments every coverage counter, and a systematic defect touching a small fraction of a large graph passes a uniform sample with near-certainty. A substrate whose scenarios were all positive, whose precision bar was a small random sample, and whose validation was recall and node/edge counts passed everything, after which an adversarial review found many systematic wrong-output bugs — precision-first was claimed in prose and verified coverage-first.
alternatives: Coverage-first verification: positive-only scenarios, recall percentages, node and edge counts, and a uniform random sample as the precision bar
Advisory rather than gating adversarial review
consequences: Easier: systematic wrong-output is caught at authoring or build time instead of by the luck of someone running a review, and the precision-first claim becomes falsifiable
Easier: the adversary catches whole bug classes the author is blind to
Harder: every emitting scenario carries a negative twin, every category carries a standing invariant test, and the definition of done gains a blind-review gate

items.title: Store pilot intent repo-local at .coredoc/intent.json
items.statement: The pilot stores intent repo-local under git; agent-authored capture goes only through the coredoc intent capture CLI, while maintainer authority and lifecycle decisions are reviewed repository edits.

payload.choice: Repo-local .coredoc/intent.json under git review; agents write only via the capture CLI, maintainers decide authority via reviewed edits
payload.question: Where does durable product intent live for the MVP, and how do agents write it
payload.rationale: Keeps durable intent outside the rebuildable graph while git carries review and history and code enforces accepted-item protection
alternatives: Native product nodes in the code graph
A parser-storage sidecar outside version control
Skill-driven hand edits of the overlay
consequences: Intent content is present in every clone and CI checkout
Central multi-repo storage is reconsidered only after pilot value is observed

items.title: Store team intent as relational rows in the cloud workspace
items.statement: Durable product intent lives as relational rows in the workspace control plane (items, tree, sources, anchors, and append-only authority transitions), never as one document blob; agents write only through propose, humans change authority only through role-gated review in a user session, and local files are deterministic projections or import artifacts.

payload.choice: Relational rows under the workspace (Postgres control plane); MCP propose for agents, role-gated user-session review for authority; local files as projections
payload.question: Where does durable product intent live for a team, and how is it written
payload.rationale: Per-item rows give concurrent review, SQL queryability, and physical tenant isolation; the graph stays the rebuildable plane anchors point into
alternatives: One JSONB overlay blob per workspace (rejected v1: whole-blob serializable rewrites, no queryability)
Repo-local git file as the permanent authority
Intent nodes inside the rebuildable code graph
consequences: Leaving team mode is an export, not a peer sync
Import is one-way onboarding with an explicit cutover marker

items.rationale: Replaces the pilot-era repo-local storage decision after the cloud redesign: git-file storage remains only as the pre-cutover stepping stone, and the rejected single-JSONB-blob model is recorded in the spec as a named anti-pattern.

items.title: A profile target is a language scope, never a workspace package
items.statement: A profile target is one language plus its include and exclude patterns and never a workspace package, so all same-language packages share one index and cross-package calls resolve.

payload.choice: A target is a language scope — one language plus the patterns that include and exclude its files — and never a workspace package. Several packages of the same language share one target and therefore one index; package topology stays internal to the engine and never sets target boundaries. Overlap between targets is guarded rather than tolerated: when two targets claim the same file the merge fails and names both.
payload.question: A multi-language repository is described by a composite profile made of targets — should a target be one workspace package, matching the repository layout, or a language scope?
payload.rationale: Cross-package call resolution depends on indexing a whole language's sources together, because the joins connecting a caller in one package to a definition in another exist only inside a single index over all of them. Splitting a language across several targets fragments that index and silently loses those edges.
alternatives: One target per workspace package, matching the on-disk layout and how people talk about the repository
Tolerating overlapping targets by duplicating the nodes of a shared file instead of failing the merge
consequences: Easier: cross-package calls within a language resolve without extra work, and a monorepo of many same-language packages needs one target rather than one per package
Harder: a per-package target is not available as a scoping device, so narrowing extraction to a single package is expressed with include patterns inside the target
Files of a known language that no target claims are reported as unclaimed scope, so a coverage gap surfaces explicitly
Reversing this would fragment the per-language index and lose cross-package resolution

items.title: Workspace release trigger mode
items.statement: Each workspace runs in one release trigger mode: manual keeps every event a maintainer action, merge records a release when a PR merges into the repository's production branch, and deploy records it from a CI step after the production deploy; the default is manual.

payload.choice: A per-workspace mode with three values, defaulting to manual so existing workspaces do not change.
payload.question: What turns a merged change into a recorded intent release?
payload.rationale: Coredoc has no deploy signal of its own; trunk-based teams equate a production-branch merge with a deploy, others deploy from CI.
alternatives: Always record on merge
Always require the CI step
consequences: Merge into any non-production branch is never a delivery
Switching back to manual stops the automatic actors without touching history

items.title: Zig file-struct as class
items.statement: A Zig file that declares at least one top-level container field is emitted as a class named from the file basename, with its top-level fields as properties and its top-level functions as methods of that class; a file without top-level fields is a namespace whose functions stay plain functions.

payload.choice: Emit the file-struct as a class when the file has at least one top-level container field; its top-level functions become methods with classId pointing at it. The @This() alias alone does not trigger the rule.
payload.question: Every Zig file is implicitly a struct. Should a file that declares fields be a graph class with its top-level functions as methods, or should top-level functions always be plain functions?
payload.rationale: Matches how Zig code names these functions and keeps nested-struct and file-struct treatment consistent.
alternatives: No synthetic file-struct node: top-level functions are plain functions everywhere and top-level fields are ignored
consequences: Method ids take the form method:<path>:<File>.<fn> for file-structs, so the rule cannot change later without an id migration
A namespace helper and a type method are distinguishable in the graph
The rule keys on observed data shape (fields present), not on file-name casing conventions

items.rationale: Zig code refers to such functions as Config.init, and the rule mirrors how functions nested in a named struct are treated. The choice fixes stable ids, so reversing it later requires an id migration.

items.title: Candidate capture flow
items.statement: An agent captures reviewed product intent into the overlay through preflight, drafting, deterministic capture, validation, and maintainer hand-off.

steps.action: Preflight the coredoc CLI for the capture subcommand
Identify the reviewed source and resolve the project id
Draft typed proposals with exact source identities in the scratchpad
Run coredoc intent capture and then validate
Report the capture summary and overlay diff to the maintainer
steps.outcome: Maintainer owns the accept or reject decision

steps.action: Stop and tell the user how to make the CLI available

payload.trigger: A finalized source is nominated for capture
payload.terminationCondition: Candidates are written and handed to the maintainer for review, or the run stops with nothing written

items.title: A Zig type is keyed on the file that declares it
items.statement: Zig types are identified by their declaring file and qualified name; aliases created through @import are not resolved to the declaring type and no edges cross into other languages in the same repository.

payload.reason: There is no symbol index for Zig and import resolution is outside this slice.
payload.affects: Mixed-language repositories and agents following a Zig alias to its definition.
payload.constraint: No cross-file type identity and no cross-language edges for Zig.

items.title: Desktop cannot mint the intent-release token
items.statement: Only the web workspace settings can mint a service token with the intent-release scope; the desktop app mints CI tokens without a scope choice.

payload.reason: The desktop token surface posts a name only and has no scope picker.
payload.affects: Maintainers who administer a workspace from the desktop app alone.
payload.constraint: Configuring deploy mode end-to-end requires the web UI or the REST API for the token.

items.title: Import onboards one overlay into an empty workspace
items.statement: Workspace intent is workspace-scoped and multi-repo, but v1 import is onboarding-only: it accepts a single project overlay into a workspace with no existing intent content, lands items on domains (the local format has no features), and never merges; additional repositories contribute intent through propose and bootstrap, not import.
items.rationale: Replaces the pilot-era single-repo-overlay limitation: multi-repo storage now exists in the workspace; the remaining limitation is the shape of the one-shot import path.

items.title: Cross-language edges inside one repository are not resolved yet
items.statement: Within a single multi-language repository, a call made in one language target to a route served by another language target is not resolved into an edge.

payload.reason: The planned resolution reuses the cross-repo linker's protocol hop applied inside a repository, and that work is deferred rather than implemented.
payload.affects: Multi-language repositories, where a frontend-to-backend call inside the same repo appears as an unresolved external call rather than reaching its handler.
payload.constraint: Protocol edges that cross language targets inside one repository are not produced; each target is parsed and merged, but no cross-language hop is composed between them.

items.title: Local intent is a stepping stone to the cloud workspace
items.statement: The repo-local overlay is an onboarding stage, not a peer authority: after a project imports into a cloud workspace, the workspace rows are the sole write authority, local intent write commands fail fast naming the owning workspace, and local files remain only as read-only projections or import/export artifacts.
items.rationale: Replaces the pilot-era 'local only, no cloud persistence' limitation: cloud persistence now exists and is the primary product path; what remains limited is the local side's role.

items.title: No deploy signal without the CI step
items.statement: Coredoc has no production-deploy signal of its own: deploy mode depends on one step in the CI pipeline after the deploy job, and merge mode treats a merge into the production branch as the deploy.

payload.reason: Deployments happen outside Coredoc; the connector observes pull requests, not runtime.
payload.affects: Workspaces whose pipeline does not run the release step, and CI systems without a GitHub connector, which use deploy mode for records and manual plans.
payload.constraint: Effectivity in deploy mode is recorded only when the pipeline runs the release step with an intent-release token; without it items stay planned after merge.

items.title: Pilot intent is local only
items.statement: The pilot stores and serves intent locally; there is no cloud sync, collaboration API, or server persistence until local value is proven.

payload.reason: Avoids a premature dual-store synchronization protocol before local value is proven
payload.affects: Every intent use case in the pilot
payload.constraint: No cloud sync, collaboration API, or server persistence in the pilot

items.title: A raw graph query is not narrowed to the caller's repositories
items.statement: Raw graph queries are not filtered by repository within the graph they open, so scope selection chooses which graph is read but never restricts what inside it is visible.

payload.reason: Arbitrary query text cannot be rewritten safely to carry a repository predicate, so the control is which graph the caller may open and whether the tool is offered at all, not a filter inside the query
payload.constraint: Once a graph is selected, a raw query reads everything in it; the repository narrowing that every fixed tool applies is not applied to raw queries, and this is stated in the tool's own description rather than being fixed by filtering

items.title: Overlay is repo-local and single-repo
items.statement: The pilot overlay lives at .coredoc/intent.json inside one repository; multi-repo and project-central storage are deferred.

payload.reason: Git provides review and history while the capture operation protects accepted items
payload.affects: Capture, review, and context for multi-repo projects
payload.constraint: One repo-local overlay file per single-repo project

items.title: Semantic search is local-only and off by default
items.statement: Semantic search over the graph is available only in a local deployment and only when explicitly enabled, so it is absent from the shared cloud tool surface.

payload.reason: It depends on locally generated embeddings and is kept off the shared multi-tenant surface, so the permanent tool roster stays uniform for every consumer.
payload.affects: Agents on the cloud MCP endpoint, and any local agent whose environment has not enabled the gate, must rely on symbol search and the explain router instead.
payload.constraint: The semantic-search tool is neither listed nor dispatchable unless its environment gate is on, and it is not part of the permanent tool set the cloud offering iterates.

items.title: Unlinked report covers one sync only
items.statement: The unlinked-repositories list in a connector sync result reflects the sync that produced it; no history of unlinked repositories is kept and no earlier sync result is amended.
items.rationale: The job result is the only surface today; a history would be a subsystem with no consumer.

items.title: Zig declarations inside grammar-error regions are not extracted
items.statement: The bundled tree-sitter Zig grammar lags the current Zig syntax, so a file whose tree contains an error region still yields its other declarations but loses those inside the error subtree.

payload.reason: The grammar is an upstream dependency bundled with tree-sitter-wasms and still reserves identifiers such as async; refreshing it is a dependency bump, not substrate work.
payload.affects: Zig repositories using syntax newer than the bundled grammar; on the reference fixture five of 575 files carried error nodes.
payload.constraint: Declarations located inside a grammar ERROR subtree are missing from the graph; the parse does not fail and the file is still counted as parsed.

items.title: Zig extraction yields types and functions only
items.statement: For Zig targets no call, import, entrypoint, data-model, database-operation or external-call edges are produced; impact and dependency tools answer empty for Zig code and the profile scorecard carries no coverage evidence for it.

payload.reason: This is the first vertical of the substrate and no semantic index exists for Zig; @import and call resolution are a later slice.
payload.affects: Maintainers and agents using find_callers, find_dependents, analyze_change_impact or the coverage scorecard on a Zig repository.
payload.constraint: Only file, package, class, enum and function nodes are emitted for Zig; every scorecard category is not applicable.

items.title: Zig grammar-error regions
items.statement: The bundled tree-sitter Zig grammar lags the current Zig syntax, so a file whose tree contains an error region still yields its other declarations but loses those inside the error subtree.

payload.reason: The grammar is an upstream dependency bundled with tree-sitter-wasms and still reserves identifiers such as async; refreshing it is a dependency bump, not substrate work.
payload.affects: Zig repositories using syntax newer than the bundled grammar; on the reference fixture 26 of 575 files carried error or missing nodes after recovery.
payload.constraint: Declarations located inside a grammar ERROR subtree are missing from the graph; the parse does not fail and the file is still counted as parsed.

items.title: Agent captures intent candidates from a reviewed source
items.statement: An agent turns a finalized spec or explicit product decision into typed candidate items with source provenance, without touching accepted intent.

payload.trigger: A spec section or product decision is finalized and the user asks to record it
preconditions: The source is reviewed and finalized
The project is resolved in coredoc.config.json
payload.successOutcome: Typed items are added or updated as candidates with stable intent ids and source provenance
failureOutcomes: Invalid or ambiguous content is reported and nothing is written
A proposal against an accepted item leaves the accepted item unchanged and is recorded as a separate candidate

items.title: Continuous integration keeps the shared graph current
items.statement: A team that wants the shared graph to follow the code adds the provided CI action, which re-parses, summarizes, and pushes on every trigger.

payload.trigger: The team wants the cloud graph updated automatically on code changes rather than by hand.
payload.primaryActor: A maintainer configuring the repository's continuous-integration pipeline.
preconditions: The repository's extraction profile is available to the cloud workspace
The pipeline holds a credential authorized to push to that workspace
payload.successOutcome: Each triggered run parses, summarizes, and pushes the repository, so the shared graph and the MCP answers built on it track the default branch.
failureOutcomes: The run has no profile for the repository and cannot parse it
The pipeline credential is missing or unauthorized and the push is rejected

items.title: Maintainer reviews candidates
items.statement: A maintainer explicitly accepts, rejects, or leaves pending each candidate; no decision is ever inferred from code, tests, or agent confidence.

payload.trigger: Candidates exist in the overlay after a capture
preconditions: The overlay file is valid and reviewable as a complete artifact
payload.successOutcome: Each candidate is explicitly marked accepted or rejected, or stays pending
failureOutcomes: An unreviewed candidate never becomes authoritative

items.title: A team shares one parsed graph through a cloud workspace
items.statement: A developer who already parses locally moves the results into a cloud workspace so teammates can query the same graph through a hosted MCP endpoint.

payload.trigger: The results are useful enough to share, and colleagues need the same code understanding.
payload.primaryActor: A workspace admin who has been running coredoc locally and now has teammates.
preconditions: A repository has been parsed locally and produced a graph
The admin has an authenticated cloud session and a workspace
payload.successOutcome: The graph lives in the shared workspace, invited members query it through the cloud MCP endpoint, and membership and roles are managed in that workspace.
failureOutcomes: The push is refused because the payload still carries source code, and the producing path must be fixed
The user is not a member of the workspace and cannot reach its graph

The connector sync result names the repositories whose pull requests were ingested unlinked

anchors.rationale: Owns the read-capture-write flow that preserves accepted items byte-for-byte.
Forces candidate authority on every proposal and refuses authority set by callers.
Implements the accepted-only default and the candidate/rejected authority filters.
Every ledger repoKey the connector writes is an intent repo key (scenario (a): unlinked pull requests are refused).
Every ledger repoKey the connector writes is an intent repo key (scenario (a): unlinked pull requests are refused).
The per-repository ordering-token comparison that refuses a late automatic release.
The pure plan-transition table the connector applies on every PR sync.
Strict schema and bounded fields are the structural half of the statements-only rule.
The gate that admits a service token only for the automatic body on a deploy-mode workspace.
The connector's automatic actor: mode gate, production-branch gate, plan lifecycle and merge-mode release.
The intent module barrel is the shared contract every overlay surface consumes.
Pre-run anchor for the intent e2e walkthrough: the generic engine that applies a declarative profile over the tree-sitter+SCIP substrate is the implementation touchpoint of this capability.

Review 2026-09-11: the registered LanguageProvider that claims .zig files for a zig target is the implementation touchpoint of this capability.
The single trailer parser every automatic actor reads the PR body through.

Resolves the production branch (repo setting or base default) that merge mode delivers into.

The flow terminates in this command; its refusals are the flow branches.
